Definition: Whether the system enables citizen payments to government for taxes, fees, licenses, fines, utility bills, and other government service charges.
Comments: No credible official evidence found of widespread person-to-government (P2G) payments (e.g., taxes/fees) being actively collected digitally via a national portal or LYPay/OnePay; searched tax authority announcements and CBL communications.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced multiple authoritative sources (Ministry of Finance Decision No. 247/2024, a Prime Ministerial decree of March 2026, and Decree No. 60 of 2026) showing active electronic collection of taxes and government revenue; escalated to full path. revised_comments: Libya has enabled electronic payment of government revenues: Decision No. 247 of 2024 introduced electronic income tax collection from 15 May 2024, and government decrees issued in March and again under Decree No. 60 of 2026 require the treasuries of all ministries and public bodies to accept electronic payment of taxes, customs duties and other dues alongside cash and certified cheques, indicating active P2G use rather than merely a plan.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: No clear, payment-specific consumer protection framework (e.g., mandatory dispute resolution/chargeback rights in law/regulation) found in public sources searched; while LYPay documentation references dispute resolution/chargebacks, no overarching consumer protection law for payments could be confirmed with credible legal sources.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced Law No. 6 of 2022 concerning Electronic Transactions, which contains specific payment consumer protection provisions (disclosure, liability allocation, error/loss reporting); escalated to full path. Score revised from 0/Unknown to 3/Yes.
revised_comments: Libya's Law No. 6 of 2022 concerning Electronic Transactions sets out specific consumer protection provisions applicable to digital payments, including mandatory disclosure of card and account terms, a minimum 15-day notice period before contract changes affecting commissions or restrictions, customer non-liability for entries resulting from unauthorised transactions once loss, theft or suspected compromise has been reported, and obligations on banks to retain transaction statements for at least ten years.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: No breach-notification requirement identified for Libya in available data-protection summaries; searched for statutory breach notification requirements and incident reporting obligations.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced DLA Piper's Data Protection Laws of the World guide, an authoritative legal source stating explicitly that there is no breach notification requirement in Libya; escalated to full path to confirm. A lower-quality secondary source (generisonline.com, appearing to be generic templated legal-marketing content not specific to Libyan legislation) claimed a 72-hour notification duty to a 'National Authority for Information Technology' but cited no identifiable law, so it was not relied upon. Score revised from 0/Unknown to 1/No.
revised_comments: Libya has no general legal requirement obliging organisations, including payment service providers, to notify users, regulators or a data protection authority of data breaches, cybersecurity incidents or unauthorised access within a specified timeframe. Libya's 2022 Electronic Transactions and Cybercrime laws address data confidentiality duties and penalties for unauthorised access but stop short of imposing a breach notification obligation; the Central Bank's new financial-sector data protection regulation (Circular No. 18 of 2025, mandatory from July 2026) covers the data lifecycle and imposes fines for violations but no breach notification duty has been documented within it.

Comments: No credible public evidence found of formal pro-poor governance mechanisms (e.g., consumer/low-income representation, inclusion mandate in governance documents) for LYPay/OnePay; searched CBL site, LYPay DevPortal, and public reporting.

revision_notes: Light check surfaced Libya's National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2025-2029, which includes a Consumer Financial Protection Pillar and an Electronic Payment Pillar with explicit inclusion mandates; escalated to full path. No evidence found of specific payment-system governance mechanisms such as reserved board seats or formal consumer/small-provider representation, so scored Partial rather than Yes. Score revised from 0/Unknown to 2/Partial.
revised_comments: The Central Bank of Libya's National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2025-2029, launched in June 2025, includes a dedicated Consumer Financial Protection Pillar (proposing a consumer financial protection unit and supporting legal framework) and an Electronic Payment Pillar committing to expand government-to-person digital payments and review payment legislation, evidencing an explicit financial inclusion mandate at national strategy level. No specific mechanism for consumer or small-provider representation within payment system operator governance bodies has been documented.

The Central Bank's Financial Inclusion Strategy 2025-2029 separately identifies accessibility barriers, such as inaccessible ATMs and limited assistive-technology compatibility in digital financial services, as a constraint to be addressed, but no payment-specific accessibility standard or disability-disaggregated coverage data has yet been published.

revised_comments: Approximately 75% of Libya's roughly 2.2 million state-sector employees (around 1.7 million people) received their salaries through the Central Bank's automated 'Your Instant Salary' (Ratbak Lahzi) system as of April 2026, up from a lower participation rate at the system's launch in September 2025. This figure covers civil service salary disbursement specifically; comprehensive data on the digitisation share of other G2P flows such as pensions and social transfers is not yet available.

revision_notes: Light check surfaced Libya Herald and LibyaReview reporting on a March 2026 CBL directive and a Bank of Commerce and Development e-Wallet product enabling foreign residents to open digital payment accounts using a passport and residency card, without a bank account; escalated to full path. Access is confirmed for documented foreign residents/workers, but no evidence found on access for undocumented refugees, asylum seekers, IDPs or stateless persons, so scored Partial rather than Yes. Score revised from 0/Unknown to 2/Partial.
revised_comments: Since March 2026 the Central Bank of Libya has directed commercial banks and e-payment providers to permit official foreign residents to hold e-wallets, and the Bank of Commerce and Development has launched Libya's first e-wallet for foreign residents and workers, accepting a passport and residency card in place of a bank account, subject to daily transfer limits of LYD 50,000 (individual-to-individual) and LYD 100,000 (individual-to-company). This provides a documented access pathway for legally resident foreigners, but there is no confirmed provision for undocumented refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons or stateless persons, who form a significant share of Libya's migrant population.
